steps.label: Do Now: Notation (1 of 2)
steps.content:
Do Now: Notation (1 of 2)

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does a postfix expression never need brackets?Show the answer

Each operator comes right after its two operands, so the order is fixed.

From the Prefix, Infix and Postfix lesson.

Total: 2 marks

walkthrough.title: Walk me through it: postfix and prefix

steps.text: A similar postfix question. Read left to right. Push each number onto the stack.
An operator takes the top two numbers. The lower one goes first: 2 ↑ 3 is 8.
Keep going: 6 / 2 is 3. Then + takes 40 and 3.
A similar prefix question: 2(c + d) - a / b. A number next to a bracket means multiply.
steps.visual: 2 * (c + d) - a / b

steps.text: Put brackets round every operation, in the order they are worked out.
Move each operator just before its two operands, from the inside out.
steps.visual: - * 2 + c d / a b

steps.text: Now do your two questions the same way.
steps.visual: stack for postfix   |   brackets, then move the operators

steps.label: Do Now: Bit Strings (2 of 2)
steps.content:
Do Now: Bit Strings (2 of 2)

Think → Pair → ShareWhy write each step as a new 5-bit string?Show the answer

All 5 bits stay in every step, so no bit is lost and each step can be checked.

From the Bit-String Flicking lesson. (a) Evaluate it. (b) Find every x: use * for a bit that can be 0 or 1.

Total: 2 marks

walkthrough.title: Walk me through it: bit strings

steps.text: A similar question: LCIRC-1 10001 OR NOT 10011 AND 11110. NOT and circulates go first.
steps.visual: LCIRC-1 10001 OR NOT 10011 AND 11110

steps.text: LCIRC-1: the left bit wraps round to the right. NOT flips every bit.
AND goes before OR, even though OR is written first.
A similar solve: RSHIFT-1 x AND 01110 = 00100. Call the bits of x abcde. RSHIFT-1 x is 0abcd.
Under a 1 in the mask, the bit must match: a = 0, b = 1, c = 0. d sits under a 0 and e falls off, so they can be anything.
steps.visual: a = 0   b = 1   c = 0   d, e: *

steps.text: Put the bits back in order with * for anything.

steps.label: Competition Practice: Contest 2 Games
steps.content:
ACSL Junior Contest 2

Competition Practice: Contest 2 Games

Year 9

  • Today: five games at full contest level. Notation Race, Bit Flick Blaster, Loop Lock, Contest Showdown, then a Mini-Contest.
  • Every game: new questions each round, harder as you go. Your best scores are saved.
Think → Pair → ShareWhy practise with games against a clock?Show the answer

The real contest is timed. Speed comes from doing many questions, and games make you do many.

steps.label: Check: Why the Tricks Work (1 of 2)
steps.content:
Check: Why the Tricks Work (1 of 2)

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does prefix put each operator before its two operands?Show the answer

It is one fixed rule, so an expression can only be read one way, with no brackets.

items.prompt: Why does a postfix operator take the top two numbers?
items.explain: Postfix writes each operator straight after its two operands, so they are the last two values on the stack.

steps.label: Check: Why the Tricks Work (2 of 2)
steps.content:
Check: Why the Tricks Work (2 of 2)

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does LSHIFT-1 bring a 0 in on the right?Show the answer

A shift keeps all 5 places. One bit falls off the left, so a 0 fills the gap.

items.prompt: Why is bit 2 of x a * in x AND 10011 = 00010?
items.explain: The mask has a 0 there. 0 AND 0 and 1 AND 0 are both 0, so that bit of x can be anything.

steps.label: Game 1: Notation Race
steps.content:
Game 1: Notation Race

Think → Pair → ShareWhy work out prefix from an operator with two numbers after it?Show the answer

They are its operands, so it can be done now. Its answer feeds the operator before it.

90 seconds. One try each. Streaks multiply your points.

steps.label: Game 2: Bit Flick Blaster
steps.content:
Game 2: Bit Flick Blaster

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does putting one x back in check a * answer?Show the answer

Every value the pattern allows must work. One that fails shows the pattern is wrong.

Find every x before the block lands. You have 3 lives.

steps.label: Game 3: Loop Lock
steps.content:
Game 3: Loop Lock

Think → Pair → ShareWhy can a sum from 1 to 100 skip tracing every turn?Show the answer

It adds 1 to 100. Pairs from each end (1 + 100, 2 + 99, ...) all have the same total.

The code for each lock is what its program outputs.

steps.label: Game 4: Contest Showdown
steps.content:
Game 4: Contest Showdown

Think → Pair → ShareWhy should your team agree an answer before you buzz?Show the answer

A wrong answer loses points and hands the question to the other team.

Team A against Team B. Buzz, then answer out loud.

steps.label: Game 5: Mini-Contest
steps.content:
Game 5: Mini-Contest

Think → Pair → ShareWhy answer every question, even one you are not sure of?Show the answer

An unsure answer can still score. A blank never can.

5 questions in contest order: 12 minutes today, 30 in the real contest.

steps.label: Plenary: Three in a Row
steps.content:
Plenary: Three in a Row

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does a card come back after you get it wrong?Show the answer

A miss resets that card, so it comes back until you get it 3 times in a row.

Get each card right 3 times in a row to master it. Every card is new each time. Your progress is saved.

y9cp_do_now.feedback: Use a stack. Push each number. An operator takes the top two numbers: the lower one goes first.
A number next to a bracket means multiply. Bracket every operation, then move each operator before its two operands.

y9cp_do_now_2.feedback: NOT and RCIRC first. Then AND, then XOR.
Write x as abcde and shift it. Under a 0 in the mask, that bit of x can be anything.
